directive: The new Roman-authorized expedition continues from its first camp while established estate administration, correspondence, and agricultural threads continue independently.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION LEAVES ITS FIRST CAMP AND ENTERS ROUGHER COUNTRY
events.body: The expedition leaves its first camp and moves beyond the ground examined on the previous day. The route becomes narrower and the party proceeds more cautiously, with the day's march shaped by the condition of the ground rather than by a fixed distance. Observations from the first camp are carried forward with the expedition records. The movement marks the first sustained advance into country that remains unfamiliar to Valerius and his companions.

events.title: A LOCAL GUIDE DISAGREES WITH AN EARLIER ROUTE ACCOUNT
events.body: A local guide gives the expedition a route account that differs from one received before departure. The disagreement concerns the condition of a crossing farther ahead rather than the existence of the route itself. The expedition scribes record both accounts separately. Valerius's party continues gathering information before committing itself to the crossing.

events.title: SPRING WORKERS REPORT A STRONGER DEMAND FOR WATER ON THE NEW TRACT
events.body: Word reaches the estate that the newly incorporated fields are drawing heavier water demand as spring work intensifies. The stewards compare the request with the watering arrangement already established for nearby smallholders. The additional work is accommodated without reopening the ownership question settled by the purchase. The report gives the estate a clearer picture of the practical demands created by the expanded acreage.

events.title: METELLUS CELER'S CORRESPONDENCE IS ADDED TO THE EXPEDITION PAPERS
events.body: A message associated with Quintus Caecilius Metellus Celer is preserved alongside the expedition correspondence. It concerns the usefulness of careful observations and the preservation of documentary material rather than directing Valerius's route. The scribes mark the message as a separate Roman political correspondence item. Its presence reinforces the continuing connection between Valerius's field activity and the Roman circles already following his affairs.

events.title: THE ESTATE'S SPRING ACCOUNTS ARE KEPT SEPARATE FROM THE EXPEDITION RECORDS
events.body: The estate administration closes another set of spring entries while the expedition remains away from the household's ordinary routine. Estate and expedition records are kept separate so that field observations cannot be confused with household accounts. The separation allows the expedition papers to accumulate independently while the estate continues its established agricultural administration. No new financial receipt is posted from the expedition during the week.

events.title: THE EXPEDITION REACHES ITS FIRST DIFFICULT PASS
events.body:
The road ahead rises gradually before narrowing into a rough passage between higher ground.

You can see from the movement of the animals that the ascent will demand more from the party than the easier country behind you.

You slow the column rather than allowing the front of the expedition to disappear beyond the next bend.

The men carrying the heavier loads are brought forward into a more manageable order, and the animals are spaced so that a stumble does not pull the rest of the line into confusion.

The passage is not impossible, but it is the first place where the country itself forces the expedition to move according to its own terms.

You climb on foot for part of the approach, examining the surface before allowing the animals to follow.

Loose stones shift beneath your sandals, and each movement has to be chosen with more care than it would on an ordinary road.

Above the first rise, you find that the passage does not simply end; it bends around the slope and continues toward a lower saddle.

The sight changes the day's calculation, because the route remains passable but will take longer than the party's earlier estimate.

You order the march to continue at the slower pace.

No one mistakes the delay for failure, because the alternative would be to force the column forward until fatigue turns a manageable obstacle into an actual accident.

The expedition reaches the saddle later in the day and pauses long enough for the animals and men to recover.

From there you can see the country on the far side of the pass, including several lower routes that were invisible from the approach.

You compare what you see with the reports gathered during the preceding days.

One local account now appears more plausible than another, but you keep both in the written record because the expedition has not yet tested the farther route itself.

Before the descent begins, you personally inspect the first section and identify a place where the party can stop if the ground worsens.

The column then moves down carefully, with the day's remaining light becoming an important limit on how far you are willing to continue.

By the time the expedition establishes its next temporary camp, the pass has become the first major geographic feature entered into the expedition record from direct observation.

You have gained no miraculous treasure and conquered no great city.

What you have gained is more practical: a tested route, a measured difficulty, and a clearer understanding of how the country constrains movement.

The expedition's record now contains its first passage whose usefulness depends on having personally crossed it, and the road beyond remains open for the next stage of the journey.

events.title: THE FIRST PASS ACCOUNT IS COPIED INTO THE EXPEDITION'S PERMANENT RECORD
events.body: The expedition scribes copy the account of the difficult pass into the permanent field record. Measurements and route observations are kept together with the local statements that preceded the crossing, allowing the written account to distinguish direct observation from testimony. The day's copy is sealed before the party prepares for the next movement. The expedition therefore ends the week with its first substantial route feature documented from direct experience.
